questions.title: Characteristic feature of the pars nervosa
questions.question: The following is a characteristic feature of the pars nervosa:

options.A: It is formed of groups of nerve cells separated by fenestrated capillaries.
options.B: It has accumulated neurosecretion called Herring bodies.
options.C: It is formed of follicles of basophilic cells with granular cytoplasm.
options.D: It has an upward extension known as the pars tuberalis.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The pars nervosa contains few or no nerve cell bodies; it is made mainly of unmyelinated axons of hypothalamic magnocellular neurons and supporting pituicytes, not groups of nerve cells around fenestrated capillaries.
explanations.B: Correct. The pars nervosa (posterior pituitary) is the storage and release site for hypothalamic hormones, and the axons reaching it show dilated terminals packed with neurosecretory granules. These accumulations are visible by light microscopy as Herring bodies. They store oxytocin or ADH bound to neurophysin, awaiting release into the fenestrated capillaries of the neurohypophysis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Follicles of basophilic cells with granular cytoplasm describe glandular adenohypophyseal tissue, not the pars nervosa, which contains no follicles.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The pars tuberalis is an upward extension of the pars distalis (adenohypophysis) around the infundibular stalk, not of the pars nervosa.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise Herring bodies as the characteristic accumulated neurosecretion of the pars nervosa.

questions.title: Stain that identifies mammotrophs
questions.question: Mammotrophs could be identified by the following stain:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Silver stains demonstrate reticular fibres and argyrophil cells of the diffuse neuroendocrine system, not pituitary mammotrophs.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Orcein is an elastic-fibre stain and is not used to demonstrate the acidophilic mammotrophs of the anterior pituitary.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Orange G selectively stains the somatotrophs (growth-hormone acidophils), not the prolactin-secreting mammotrophs.
explanations.D: Correct. Mammotrophs (lactotrophs) are the prolactin-secreting acidophils of the pars distalis, and among the acidophils they are demonstrated with carmine (erythrosin or carmine), which distinguishes them from the orange-G-positive somatotrophs. This selective affinity lets the two acidophil populations be told apart in stained sections. Their number and granularity increase markedly during pregnancy and lactation.

questions.learning_objective: Identify carmine as the selective stain for prolactin-secreting mammotrophs, distinct from orange-G somatotrophs.

questions.title: Common feature of the diffuse neuroendocrine system
questions.question: A common feature of the cells of the diffuse neuro-endocrine system (DNES) is that they:

options.C: Are rich in sER and lysosomes.

explanations.A: Incorrect. DNES cells arise from several germ layers, many from neural crest and neuroectoderm as well as endoderm, so a single endodermal origin is not their common feature.
explanations.B: Incorrect. DNES cells are defined by abundant membrane-bound dense-core secretory granules storing peptides and amines, so being granule-free is the opposite of the truth.
explanations.C: Incorrect. They are not characterised chiefly by smooth ER and lysosomes; their hallmark is amine-precursor uptake and decarboxylation with dense-core granule storage.
explanations.D: Correct. The diffuse neuroendocrine system (formerly called APUD) is a scattered population of amine- and peptide-secreting cells that share key properties with neurons: they take up amine precursors, decarboxylate them, and store the products in dense-core granules for regulated release. Because of this shared biochemistry and secretory behaviour they are regarded as highly modified neurons. Many indeed derive from the neural crest.

questions.learning_objective: State that DNES cells behave as highly modified neurons sharing the amine-handling and granule-storage properties of neurons.

questions.title: Development of the pituitary gland
questions.question: Regarding the development of the pituitary gland, mark the one correct statement:

options.A: The infundibulum arises as a mesodermal diverticulum from the roof of the diencephalon.
options.B: The infundibulum forms the anterior lobe of the pituitary gland.
options.C: Rathke's pouch is an endodermal diverticulum from the floor of the stomodeum.
options.D: It is derived from two sources: the infundibulum and Rathke's pouch.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The infundibulum is a neuroectodermal, not mesodermal, downgrowth from the floor of the diencephalon, so both the germ layer and the site are wrong here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The infundibulum forms the posterior lobe (neurohypophysis) and stalk, not the anterior lobe.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Rathke's pouch is an ectodermal diverticulum from the roof of the stomodeum (primitive mouth), not an endodermal outgrowth from its floor.
explanations.D: Correct. The hypophysis has a dual origin: an ectodermal outpocketing of the stomodeal roof (Rathke's pouch) forms the adenohypophysis (anterior lobe, pars intermedia and pars tuberalis), while a neuroectodermal downgrowth from the floor of the diencephalon (the infundibulum) forms the neurohypophysis (posterior lobe and stalk). These two primordia meet and fuse to build the definitive gland. This is why the pituitary has both a glandular and a neural part.

questions.learning_objective: Explain the dual embryological origin of the pituitary from Rathke's pouch and the infundibulum.

questions.title: Cells spared in cryptorchidism
questions.question: In cryptorchidism (undescended testes), the following cells are not affected:
questions.subject: androl

explanations.A: Incorrect. Primary spermatocytes belong to the temperature-sensitive germ-cell line and are damaged when the testis remains at core body temperature.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Spermatids are late germ cells and are among the first to be lost when spermatogenesis fails in an undescended testis.
explanations.C: Correct. In cryptorchidism the seminiferous (germinal) epithelium is exposed to the higher intra-abdominal temperature, which arrests and destroys the temperature-sensitive spermatogenic cells. The interstitial Leydig cells, which secrete testosterone, are relatively resistant to this heat and are spared, so androgen production and secondary sexual characters are usually preserved. This is why an untreated undescended testis causes infertility but not necessarily hypoandrogenism.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Secondary spermatocytes are germ cells formed during meiosis and are also lost when the heat-sensitive spermatogenic line is damaged.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that cryptorchidism damages heat-sensitive germ cells while sparing the interstitial Leydig cells.

questions.title: Least likely effect of chronic androgen abuse
questions.question: Chronic androgen abuse by healthy male athletes is least likely to result in:
questions.subject: androl

explanations.A: Incorrect. Androgens stimulate renal erythropoietin and the bone marrow, so chronic abuse tends to raise the red-cell mass, making increased erythropoiesis an expected effect.
explanations.B: Correct. Exogenous androgens suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis by negative feedback, lowering GnRH and therefore LH and FSH. Without adequate intratesticular testosterone and FSH support, spermatogenesis declines and the sperm count falls rather than rises. This is why anabolic-steroid abuse is a recognised cause of male infertility and testicular atrophy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. By raising haemoglobin and muscle mass, androgen abuse can improve physical endurance, so a rise in endurance is an expected rather than a least-likely result.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The classic sought-after effect of androgen abuse is anabolic growth of skeletal muscle, so increased muscle mass is expected.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that exogenous androgens suppress the HPG axis and reduce sperm count despite their anabolic effects.

questions.title: Ovarian hilar cells
questions.question: Concerning the ovarian hilar cells, they:

options.A: Are located in the ovarian cortex.
options.B: Are structurally related to Sertoli cells.

questions.subject: gyn

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hilar cells lie in the ovarian hilum, the medulla/hilus region where vessels enter, not in the cortex.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hilar cells are the ovarian counterpart of the testicular interstitial (Leydig) cells, not of Sertoli cells.
explanations.C: Correct. Ovarian hilar cells are steroidogenic cells in the hilum that are homologous to testicular Leydig cells, and like Leydig cells they contain rod-shaped cytoplasmic Reinke's crystalloids. They secrete androgens, and their hyperplasia or tumours can cause virilisation. Their presence and crystalloids are the histological clue to their Leydig-cell nature.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hilar cells secrete androgens like Leydig cells; progesterone is the product of the corpus luteum granulosa-lutein cells, not of hilar cells.

questions.learning_objective: Identify ovarian hilar cells as Leydig-cell homologues containing Reinke's crystalloids and secreting androgens.

questions.title: Function of the syncytiotrophoblast
questions.question: Choose the correct statement regarding the syncytiotrophoblast:

options.A: It is responsible for the secretion of placental hormones.
options.B: It is formed of pale-stained cells.
options.D: It disappears after the 4th month of pregnancy.

questions.subject: obs

explanations.A: Correct. The syncytiotrophoblast is the outer multinucleated layer of the placental villus in direct contact with maternal blood, and it is the main endocrine tissue of the placenta. It synthesises and secretes the placental hormones, including human chorionic gonadotropin, human placental lactogen, progesterone and estrogens. It also carries out maternofetal exchange across its microvillous surface.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The syncytiotrophoblast has darkly stained, densely packed nuclei and cytoplasm; it is the underlying cytotrophoblast (Langhans cells) that appears pale.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Its maternal-facing surface bears abundant microvilli, a brush border that greatly increases the area for exchange, so it is not devoid of microvilli.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The syncytiotrophoblast persists throughout pregnancy as the exchange and endocrine surface; it is the cytotrophoblast that becomes discontinuous in later pregnancy.

questions.learning_objective: State that the syncytiotrophoblast is the endocrine layer of the placenta secreting hCG, hPL and steroid hormones.

questions.title: Lateral wall of the ischiorectal fossa
questions.question: The lateral wall of the ischiorectal fossa is formed by:

options.D: The obturator internus muscle and its fascia.

questions.subject: fnd

explanations.A: Incorrect. The levator ani with its fascia forms the sloping medial wall and roof of the ischiorectal fossa, not the lateral wall.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The external anal sphincter lies medially around the anal canal, contributing to the medial wall, not the lateral wall.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The internal anal sphincter is a thickening of the bowel's own circular muscle around the anal canal and is not a wall of the ischiorectal fossa.
explanations.D: Correct. The ischiorectal (ischio-anal) fossa is a wedge-shaped space lateral to the anal canal, and its lateral wall is formed by the obturator internus muscle covered by its fascia, together with the lower part of the ischial tuberosity. The pudendal canal (Alcock's canal), carrying the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels, runs within this fascia on the lateral wall. The medial wall, by contrast, is the levator ani and the external anal sphincter.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the obturator internus and its fascia as the lateral wall of the ischiorectal fossa carrying the pudendal canal.

questions.title: What the pelvic diaphragm separates
questions.question: The pelvic diaphragm separates the:

options.A: True pelvis from the false pelvis.
options.C: Deep perineal pouch from the superficial perineal pouch.

questions.subject: fnd

explanations.A: Incorrect. The true pelvis is separated from the false pelvis by the pelvic brim (inlet), not by the pelvic diaphragm.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The ischiorectal fossa lies within the perineum below the pelvic diaphragm; the diaphragm does not separate the perineum from that fossa.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The deep and superficial perineal pouches are separated from each other by the perineal membrane, not by the pelvic diaphragm.
explanations.D: Correct. The pelvic diaphragm, formed by the levator ani and coccygeus muscles with their fasciae, is the muscular floor of the pelvic cavity. It separates the pelvic cavity above from the perineum below. Structures such as the anal canal and the urethra pass through it to reach the perineum.

questions.learning_objective: State that the pelvic diaphragm separates the pelvic cavity from the perineum.

questions.title: Ligament of the ovary
questions.question: Which of the following is a ligament of the ovary?
questions.subject: gyn

explanations.A: Correct. The suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament) is a peritoneal fold that attaches the ovary to the lateral pelvic wall and transmits the ovarian vessels, nerves and lymphatics. It is a true ligament of the ovary, along with the ligament of the ovary proper and the mesovarium. It is ligated when removing the ovary because it carries the ovarian artery.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The utero-vesical fold is a peritoneal reflection between the uterus and bladder; it is not a ligament of the ovary.
explanations.C: Incorrect. There is no named utero-rectal ligament of the ovary; the recto-uterine (uterosacral) folds relate the cervix to the sacrum.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The broad ligament is a ligament of the uterus that encloses the tube and suspends the ovary through the mesovarium, but it is not itself the ovarian ligament.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the suspensory ligament as a true ligament of the ovary transmitting the ovarian vessels.

questions.title: Origin of the ovarian arteries
questions.question: The ovarian arteries originate from:

options.B: The abdominal aorta just below the renal arteries.
options.C: The abdominal aorta above the renal arteries.

questions.subject: gyn

explanations.A: Incorrect. The ovarian arteries do not arise from the renal arteries, which supply the kidneys.
explanations.B: Correct. The ovarian arteries arise directly from the front of the abdominal aorta a short distance below the origin of the renal arteries, at about the level of L2. They descend retroperitoneally and reach the ovary through the suspensory ligament. Their high origin reflects the ovary's development high on the posterior abdominal wall before its descent into the pelvis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The ovarian arteries arise below, not above, the renal arteries.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The internal iliac artery supplies the uterus through the uterine artery and much of the pelvis, but the ovarian artery comes from the aorta, not the internal iliac.

questions.learning_objective: State that the ovarian artery arises from the abdominal aorta just below the renal arteries.

field_notes.kasr: 2023 EOM 195, p.8 (option C reworded for a clean single-best answer, key unchanged)

questions.title: Part of the broad ligament supporting the uterine tube
questions.question: The part of the broad ligament giving attachment and support to the uterine tube is called the:
questions.subject: gyn

explanations.A: Incorrect. The mesometrium is the largest part of the broad ligament below the mesovarium, related to the body of the uterus, not to the tube.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The mesovarium is the short posterior fold that suspends the ovary, not the uterine tube.
explanations.C: Correct. The mesosalpinx is the upper free part of the broad ligament lying between the uterine (fallopian) tube above and the ovary and mesovarium below. It encloses and supports the uterine tube and contains the epoophoron and the anastomosing tubal branches of the ovarian and uterine vessels. Salpinx means tube, which is the clue to its name.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The round ligament of the uterus runs from the uterine cornu to the labium majus through the inguinal canal; it is not a supporting mesentery of the tube.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the mesosalpinx as the part of the broad ligament enclosing and supporting the uterine tube.

questions.title: Hormones derived from tyrosine
questions.question: Which of the following hormones are derived from one amino acid (tyrosine)?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cortisol is a steroid hormone synthesised from cholesterol, not from an amino acid.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid steroid derived from cholesterol.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Parathyroid hormone is a polypeptide of 84 amino acids, not a single-amino-acid derivative.
explanations.D: Correct. The thyroid hormones T3 and T4 are amine hormones synthesised from the amino acid tyrosine, which is iodinated and coupled within thyroglobulin. The catecholamines are also tyrosine derivatives, so tyrosine is the shared precursor of this amine class. This distinguishes thyroid hormones from the steroid (cholesterol-derived) and peptide hormones.

questions.learning_objective: Classify thyroid hormones as amine hormones derived from the amino acid tyrosine.

questions.title: G protein-linked hormone receptors
questions.question: Which of the following is correct as regards the G protein-linked hormone receptors?

options.A: In the active state, the alpha subunit bound to GTP dissociates from the G protein.
options.B: They are activated by steroid hormones to increase the enzyme activity of protein synthesis.
options.C: They are proteins that pass the membrane only once and function directly as enzymes.
options.D: In the active state, the beta subunit dissociates from the beta-gamma complex to associate with other signalling proteins.

explanations.A: Correct. When an agonist binds a G-protein-coupled receptor, the receptor catalyses exchange of GDP for GTP on the alpha subunit of the heterotrimeric G protein. The GTP-bound alpha subunit then dissociates from the beta-gamma dimer and goes on to regulate effector enzymes such as adenylyl cyclase or phospholipase C. Hydrolysis of GTP back to GDP terminates the signal and lets the subunits reassociate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Steroid hormones act on intracellular nuclear receptors, not on membrane G-protein-coupled receptors.
explanations.C: Incorrect. GPCRs are seven-transmembrane (serpentine) proteins that signal through a G protein; single-pass receptors that are themselves enzymes describe the catalytic receptor-tyrosine-kinase class.
explanations.D: Incorrect. It is the alpha subunit bound to GTP that dissociates from the beta-gamma complex to signal; the beta-gamma dimer stays together.

questions.learning_objective: Describe activation of a GPCR by dissociation of the GTP-bound alpha subunit from the beta-gamma dimer.

questions.title: Site of 25-hydroxylation of cholecalciferol
questions.question: The site of 25-hydroxylation of cholecalciferol is the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The kidney performs the second, 1-alpha-hydroxylation step that yields the active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, not the 25-hydroxylation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The skin is where 7-dehydrocholesterol is converted to cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) by ultraviolet light, before any hydroxylation.
explanations.C: Correct. Cholecalciferol undergoes its first hydroxylation at carbon 25 in the liver, producing 25-hydroxycholecalciferol (calcidiol), the main circulating and storage form. This step is not tightly regulated, so plasma 25-OH-D reflects vitamin D status. The subsequent 1-alpha-hydroxylation in the kidney is the regulated, activating step.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lung has no role in vitamin D hydroxylation.

questions.module_subject: 207 END > Physiology > Calcium and vitamin D
questions.learning_objective: State that 25-hydroxylation of cholecalciferol occurs in the liver, forming calcidiol.

questions.title: Active form of vitamin D
questions.question: The active form of vitamin D is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) is the inactive precursor formed in the skin; it must be hydroxylated twice to become active.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 24,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is generally regarded as an inactive degradation metabolite, not the active hormone.
explanations.C: Correct. The biologically active form of vitamin D is 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (calcitriol), produced by 1-alpha-hydroxylation of the 25-OH precursor in the kidney. It acts on intestine, bone and kidney to raise plasma calcium and phosphate. Its formation is stimulated by parathyroid hormone and by low plasma phosphate.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 25-hydroxyvitamin D (calcidiol) is the major circulating form but is only weakly active; it is the substrate for renal activation.

questions.module_subject: 207 END > Physiology > Calcium and vitamin D
questions.learning_objective: Identify 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol) as the active hormonal form of vitamin D.

questions.title: Pancreatic cells secreting glucagon
questions.question: Glucagon is secreted by which cells of the pancreas?

explanations.A: Correct. Glucagon is secreted by the alpha (A) cells of the pancreatic islets of Langerhans. These cells respond to hypoglycaemia by releasing glucagon, which raises blood glucose through hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. In the human islet they lie mainly at the periphery.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Beta cells secrete insulin, together with amylin and C-peptide, not glucagon.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Delta cells secrete somatostatin.
explanations.D: Incorrect. G cells secrete gastrin and are found mainly in the gastric antrum; they are not the islet source of glucagon.

questions.learning_objective: State that pancreatic alpha cells secrete glucagon.

questions.title: Cell with organelle-rich basophilic cytoplasm and secretory granules
questions.question: Basophilic cytoplasm rich in mitochondria, Golgi apparatus, rER and secretory granules is a characteristic feature of which of the following?

explanations.A: Correct. Pinealocytes are the principal secretory cells of the pineal gland and have a basophilic cytoplasm packed with mitochondria, a well-developed Golgi apparatus, rough endoplasmic reticulum and membrane-bound secretory granules for melatonin production. Their organelle-rich cytoplasm reflects active synthesis and secretion. Long cytoplasmic processes end in bulbous expansions near the fenestrated capillaries.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Spongiocytes are the cells of the adrenal zona fasciculata; their cytoplasm is pale and vacuolated (spongy) from abundant lipid droplets and smooth ER for steroidogenesis, not basophilic and granule-rich.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Herring bodies are not cells; they are dilated axon terminals in the pars nervosa storing neurosecretion, so they cannot display this organelle-rich cell cytoplasm.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Oxyphil cells of the parathyroid are acidophilic and crammed almost entirely with mitochondria, lacking the prominent rER, Golgi and secretory granules described here.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the pinealocyte as the organelle-rich, basophilic secretory cell producing melatonin.

questions.title: Most susceptible zone for prostatic carcinoma
questions.question: The acini most susceptible to prostatic carcinoma are located in the:
questions.subject: androl

explanations.A: Correct. About 70% of prostatic adenocarcinomas arise in the peripheral zone, the outer glandular zone that lies posteriorly and is palpable on digital rectal examination. This peripheral location is why the tumour is often detectable by rectal palpation and sampled by needle biopsy. It contrasts with benign prostatic hyperplasia, which arises in the transitional zone.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The transitional zone around the urethra is the usual site of benign prostatic hyperplasia, not the commonest site of carcinoma.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The central zone surrounding the ejaculatory ducts is relatively resistant and is an uncommon site of primary carcinoma.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The urethra is not a glandular zone of the prostate and is not where prostatic acinar carcinoma originates.

questions.learning_objective: State that prostatic carcinoma most often arises in the peripheral zone, unlike hyperplasia in the transitional zone.

questions.title: Histological feature of the seminal vesicle
questions.question: Which of the following is a histological feature of the seminal vesicle?

options.A: Its lining cell activity depends on the inhibin level.
options.B: Its lining epithelium is stratified columnar ciliated.
options.C: Its musculosa is formed of three layers.
options.D: Its mucosa is highly folded to provide a wide surface area for secretion.

questions.subject: androl

explanations.A: Incorrect. The secretory activity of the seminal-vesicle epithelium depends on testosterone, not on inhibin.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lining is a pseudostratified or simple columnar non-ciliated epithelium, not stratified columnar ciliated.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The muscularis of the seminal vesicle has two layers, an inner circular and an outer longitudinal, not three.
explanations.D: Correct. The seminal vesicle has an extensively folded mucosa forming a network of thin primary, secondary and tertiary folds that greatly increase the secretory surface for its fructose-rich alkaline fluid. The lining is a pseudostratified or simple columnar epithelium whose secretory activity is androgen (testosterone) dependent. Its wall has only two smooth-muscle layers, an inner circular and an outer longitudinal.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise the highly folded, androgen-dependent mucosa of the seminal vesicle.

questions.title: Feature of the secretory phase of the menstrual cycle
questions.question: The secretory phase of the menstrual cycle is characterised by:

options.A: It is under the control of FSH.
options.B: At its end the endometrial thickness reaches 2-3 cm.
options.C: Spiral arteries do not extend to the upper third of the endometrium.
options.D: Glycogen is accumulated in the cells lining the endometrial glands.

questions.subject: gyn

explanations.A: Incorrect. The secretory phase is controlled by progesterone from the corpus luteum, whereas FSH drives the earlier follicular (proliferative) phase.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The endometrium thickens to only about 5-6 mm, not 2-3 cm, at the end of the secretory phase.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The spiral (coiled) arteries lengthen and do extend into the superficial functional layer during the secretory phase.
explanations.D: Correct. The secretory (luteal) phase follows ovulation and is driven by progesterone from the corpus luteum. The endometrial gland cells accumulate glycogen, first as sub-nuclear then supra-nuclear vacuoles, and the glands become tortuous and secrete a glycogen-rich fluid that would nourish an implanting blastocyst. This secretory transformation is the histological hallmark of the phase.

questions.learning_objective: Identify glandular glycogen accumulation under progesterone as the hallmark of the secretory phase.

questions.title: Structure that is not a content of the deep perineal pouch
questions.question: The following is NOT a content of the deep perineal pouch:
questions.subject: fnd

explanations.A: Incorrect. The bulbo-urethral (Cowper's) glands lie within the deep perineal pouch in the male, so they are a content of it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The sphincter urethrae is a principal muscle of the deep perineal pouch.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The deep transversus perinei muscle lies within the deep perineal pouch.
explanations.D: Correct. The deep perineal pouch lies between the perineal membrane below and the fascia of the pelvic diaphragm above, and it contains the sphincter urethrae and deep transversus perinei muscles, the bulbo-urethral glands and membranous urethra in the male, and the internal pudendal vessels and dorsal nerve of the penis. The spongy (penile) part of the urethra runs within the corpus spongiosum in the penis and superficial pouch, so it is not a content of the deep pouch. This is why it is the exception in the list.

questions.learning_objective: List the contents of the deep perineal pouch and recognise the spongy urethra as excluded.

questions.title: Inferior relation of the pituitary gland
questions.question: Inferiorly, the pituitary gland is related to the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The temporal lobes lie lateral and superior to the region and are not the direct inferior relation of the gland.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The cavernous sinuses are lateral relations of the pituitary, not inferior.
explanations.C: Correct. The pituitary gland sits in the hypophyseal fossa (sella turcica) of the body of the sphenoid bone, and the floor of the fossa separates it from the sphenoidal air sinus that lies directly below. This close relation is the basis of the trans-sphenoidal surgical approach to pituitary tumours through the nose and sphenoid sinus. Laterally the gland relates to the cavernous sinuses and superiorly to the optic chiasma.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The orbital cavity is anterolateral to the sphenoid body and is not the inferior relation of the gland.

questions.learning_objective: State that the sphenoidal air sinus lies immediately inferior to the pituitary fossa, the basis of the trans-sphenoidal approach.

questions.title: False statement about the broad ligament
questions.question: Regarding the broad ligament, which of the following statements is FALSE?

options.A: It has the ovary attached to its anterior margin.
options.B: It has the fallopian tube at its upper border.
options.C: It contains remnants of the mesonephric tubules.
options.D: It extends from the uterus to the lateral wall of the pelvis.

questions.subject: gyn

explanations.A: Correct (this is the false statement). The ovary is attached to the POSTERIOR layer of the broad ligament by the mesovarium, not to its anterior margin. Placing the ovary on the anterior margin is therefore incorrect, which is why this statement is the one to be selected as false. The uterine tube, by contrast, occupies the free upper margin.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this statement is true). The uterine (fallopian) tube runs in the free upper border of the broad ligament.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this statement is true). The broad ligament contains mesonephric (Wolffian) remnants such as the epoophoron and paroophoron.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this statement is true). The broad ligament is a peritoneal fold extending from the side of the uterus to the lateral wall and floor of the pelvis.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that the ovary attaches to the posterior, not anterior, layer of the broad ligament.

questions.title: True statement about the ligaments of the urinary bladder
questions.question: Regarding the ligaments of the urinary bladder, which of the following is true?

options.A: The pubovesical ligaments connect the superior surface of the bladder with the pubic bone.
options.B: The pubovesical ligaments connect the neck of the bladder with the pubic bone.
options.C: The cardinal ligaments are the true ligaments of the bladder.
options.D: The broad ligament is the supporting ligament of the bladder.

questions.subject: fnd

explanations.A: Incorrect. The pubovesical ligaments attach to the neck of the bladder, not to its superior surface, which is covered by peritoneum.
explanations.B: Correct. The pubovesical ligaments (in the female) are condensations of pelvic fascia that connect the neck of the bladder to the back of the pubic bones; the male equivalent is the puboprostatic ligament. They are true fascial ligaments that anchor the bladder neck, and weakening of this support contributes to stress incontinence. They attach to the neck, not the superior surface, of the bladder.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The cardinal (transverse cervical) ligaments support the cervix and vaginal vault, not the bladder.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The broad ligament is a peritoneal fold related to the uterus and adnexa, not a ligament of the bladder.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the pubovesical ligament as connecting the bladder neck to the pubis.

questions.title: Feature of the prostatic urethra
questions.question: The prostatic urethra has the following feature:

options.A: The urethral crest is located in the anterior wall.
options.B: The ejaculatory ducts open in the anterior wall.
options.C: The ejaculatory ducts open on either side of the utricle opening.
options.D: It is the narrowest and least dilatable part of the urethra.

questions.subject: androl

explanations.A: Incorrect. The urethral crest lies on the posterior wall of the prostatic urethra, not the anterior wall.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The ejaculatory ducts open on the posterior wall beside the utricle, not on the anterior wall.
explanations.C: Correct. On the posterior wall of the prostatic urethra the urethral crest bears a midline elevation, the seminal colliculus (verumontanum), on which the prostatic utricle opens; the two ejaculatory ducts open on either side of the utricle opening. This is where the seminal-vesicle and vas-deferens secretions enter the urethra. The many prostatic ducts open into the prostatic sinuses that flank the crest.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The prostatic urethra is the widest and most dilatable part of the male urethra; the membranous part is the narrowest.

questions.learning_objective: Locate the ejaculatory-duct openings beside the prostatic utricle on the urethral crest.

questions.title: Correct statement about intercellular communication
questions.question: Regarding intercellular communication, which of the following is correct?

options.A: Neurotransmitters are secreted by endocrine glands.
options.B: Neuroendocrine hormones are released by ductless glands into synaptic junctions.
options.C: Paracrines are secreted into the extracellular fluid and act on distant organs.
options.D: Cytokines can function as autocrines, paracrines or endocrine hormones.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Neurotransmitters are released by neurons at synapses, not secreted by endocrine glands.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Neuroendocrine hormones are released by neurons into the blood, not into synaptic junctions.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Paracrines act on neighbouring cells in the immediate vicinity; action on distant organs is the endocrine mode.
explanations.D: Correct. Cytokines are signalling peptides that are not restricted to one mode of action: the same cytokine can act back on the cell that secreted it (autocrine), on neighbouring cells (paracrine), or travel in the blood to act on distant targets (endocrine). This versatility distinguishes them from classic neurotransmitters and lets them coordinate immune and endocrine responses. Their mode of action depends on context rather than on a fixed gland-to-target route.

questions.learning_objective: State that cytokines can act as autocrine, paracrine or endocrine signals.

questions.title: Long-loop negative feedback control of growth hormone
questions.question: Which of the following describes the long-loop negative feedback control of growth hormone?

options.C: IGF-1 stimulates the hypothalamus to secrete GHRH that stimulates GH secretion.
options.D: IGF-1 stimulates the hypothalamus to secrete GHIH (somatostatin) that inhibits GH secretion.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Growth hormone acting back on GHRH is a short-loop feedback, not the long loop that involves IGF-1.
explanations.B: Incorrect. GHRH inhibiting its own secretion is an ultrashort-loop, not the long loop.
explanations.C: Incorrect. IGF-1 inhibits rather than stimulates GH output, and stimulating GHRH would raise GH, which is not negative feedback.
explanations.D: Correct. In the long-loop feedback, growth hormone acts on the liver to release insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1, somatomedin C), and rising IGF-1 feeds back on the hypothalamus to stimulate growth-hormone-inhibiting hormone (GHIH, somatostatin), which suppresses further GH release from the anterior pituitary. IGF-1 also directly inhibits the somatotrophs. This closes the loop that keeps GH and IGF-1 within limits.

questions.learning_objective: Describe IGF-1-driven long-loop feedback that raises somatostatin to inhibit GH.

questions.title: Order of steps in thyroid hormone synthesis
questions.question: Which of the following is the normal sequence of steps in the thyroid gland that forms thyroid hormones?

options.A: First coupling of tyrosines, then oxidation of iodide, then iodination.
options.B: First endocytosis of thyroglobulin, then coupling, then the iodide pump.
options.C: First the iodide pump, then oxidation and iodination, then coupling of iodotyrosines.
options.D: First release of T3 and T4, then coupling, then oxidation of iodide.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Coupling is the last step, not the first; oxidation and iodination precede it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Endocytosis of thyroglobulin is part of hormone release, not the first synthetic step, and the iodide pump comes first.
explanations.C: Correct. Thyroid hormone synthesis proceeds in order: first the basal iodide (Na/I symporter) pump traps iodide from the blood into the follicular cell; then thyroid peroxidase oxidises the iodide and uses it to iodinate tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin (organification) forming MIT and DIT; finally these iodotyrosines are coupled to form T3 and T4 within the thyroglobulin. Endocytosis and proteolytic release of T3 and T4 occur later on demand.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Release of T3 and T4 is the final secretory event, not the first step.

questions.learning_objective: Order thyroid hormone synthesis: iodide trapping, oxidation/iodination, then coupling.

questions.title: Feature of thyroid hormone deficiency
questions.question: Which of the following is correct regarding thyroid hormone deficiency?

options.A: It produces a mentally and sexually normal cretin child.
options.B: It produces an increased metabolic rate.
options.C: It is accompanied by decreased body weight.
options.D: It produces coarse skin with non-pitting oedema.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Untreated congenital hypothyroidism (cretinism) causes marked mental and growth retardation, not a normal child.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Thyroid deficiency lowers, not raises, the basal metabolic rate.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hypothyroid patients tend to gain weight because of the reduced metabolic rate, not lose it.
explanations.D: Correct. Hypothyroidism in the adult (myxoedema) causes accumulation of hydrophilic glycosaminoglycans in the dermis and other tissues, drawing in water and producing a characteristic coarse, dry skin with a non-pitting (mucinous) oedema of the face and hands. The low metabolic rate also causes weight gain, cold intolerance and mental slowing. In infancy untreated deficiency causes cretinism with mental and growth retardation.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise coarse skin with non-pitting (myxoedematous) oedema as a sign of hypothyroidism.

questions.title: Calcium distribution in the body
questions.question: Which of the following is correct regarding calcium distribution in the body?

options.A: The labile readily exchangeable pool represents 99% of total body calcium.
options.B: The stable pool in mature bone represents 1% of total body calcium.
options.C: The large stable bone pool is readily exchangeable with plasma calcium.
options.D: Plasma calcium is about 10 mg/dl and exists in both diffusible and non-diffusible forms.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The 99% figure refers to the stable calcium of bone, not the small labile exchangeable pool.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The mature stable bone pool holds the great majority (about 99%) of body calcium, not 1%.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The large mineralised bone pool is stable and only slowly exchangeable; only a small surface pool exchanges readily with plasma.
explanations.D: Correct. Total plasma calcium is normally about 10 mg/dl and circulates in two broad forms: a diffusible fraction (ionised free calcium plus calcium complexed to small anions), which is filterable and physiologically active, and a non-diffusible fraction bound to plasma proteins, mainly albumin. Only the ionised portion is biologically active and hormonally regulated. About 99% of body calcium is stored in bone, most of it in a stable, non-readily-exchangeable pool.

questions.learning_objective: State that plasma calcium (~10 mg/dl) exists in diffusible and protein-bound non-diffusible forms.

questions.title: Effect of physiological parathyroid hormone
questions.question: Physiological levels of parathyroid hormone induce:

explanations.A: Incorrect. PTH raises, not lowers, plasma calcium, so it causes hypercalcaemia rather than hypocalcaemia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. PTH increases urinary phosphate (phosphaturia); it does not cause hypophosphaturia.
explanations.C: Correct. Parathyroid hormone lowers plasma phosphate by inhibiting phosphate reabsorption in the proximal renal tubule, producing phosphaturia and hence hypophosphataemia. At the same time it raises plasma calcium through bone resorption, distal renal calcium reabsorption and vitamin-D-mediated intestinal absorption. The net picture of PTH action is a high plasma calcium with a low plasma phosphate.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Physiological PTH enhances distal tubular calcium reabsorption and therefore tends to reduce urinary calcium, opposite to hypercalciuria.

questions.learning_objective: State that PTH is phosphaturic and produces hypophosphataemia while raising plasma calcium.

questions.title: Effect of cortisol on metabolism
questions.question: What is an effect of cortisol on metabolism?

explanations.A: Correct. Cortisol is a glucocorticoid whose central metabolic action is to raise blood glucose by stimulating hepatic gluconeogenesis, supplying substrate by mobilising amino acids from muscle protein breakdown and fatty acids from adipose tissue. It also reduces peripheral glucose uptake, reinforcing its hyperglycaemic, catabolic profile. This is why chronic excess produces steroid-induced diabetes and muscle wasting.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cortisol favours lipolysis and fat redistribution rather than net lipogenesis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cortisol is catabolic in muscle, promoting protein breakdown, not anabolism.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cortisol raises blood glucose and opposes glucose utilisation; it does not primarily drive glycolysis.

questions.learning_objective: State that cortisol raises blood glucose by stimulating hepatic gluconeogenesis.

questions.title: Tissue where insulin is required for glucose entry
questions.question: Insulin is essential for glucose entry into which of the following?

explanations.A: Correct. Skeletal muscle and adipose tissue take up glucose mainly through the insulin-responsive GLUT4 transporter, so insulin is required to translocate GLUT4 to the membrane and allow glucose entry. This is why insulin deficiency chiefly impairs muscle and fat glucose uptake. Resting muscle is therefore an insulin-dependent tissue.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Neurons take up glucose through insulin-independent GLUT3 and GLUT1, so brain glucose entry does not require insulin.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Renal tubular cells absorb glucose by sodium-glucose cotransport and GLUT2, independent of insulin.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pancreatic beta cells sense glucose through insulin-independent GLUT2/GLUT1 uptake, not by an insulin-dependent route.

questions.learning_objective: Identify skeletal muscle as an insulin-dependent (GLUT4) tissue for glucose uptake.

questions.title: Correct statement about spermatogenesis
questions.question: Which of the following is correct regarding spermatogenesis?

options.B: Spermatogenesis needs an optimum testicular temperature of about 32 C.
options.C: Exposure to strong irradiation stimulates the seminiferous tubules.
options.D: Androgens are not essential for spermatogenesis.

questions.subject: androl

explanations.A: Incorrect. Inhibin from Sertoli cells inhibits, rather than stimulates, FSH secretion by negative feedback.
explanations.B: Correct. Normal spermatogenesis requires a testicular temperature a few degrees below core body temperature, about 32-35 C, which the scrotum, the pampiniform-plexus counter-current heat exchange, and the cremaster and dartos muscles maintain. Raising the temperature, as in cryptorchidism or fever, arrests the heat-sensitive germ cells and impairs fertility. This temperature dependence is the basis of scrotal cooling of the testes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ionising radiation damages the rapidly dividing spermatogenic cells; it does not stimulate the seminiferous tubules.
explanations.D: Incorrect. High intratesticular testosterone (androgen) is essential for spermatogenesis to proceed.

questions.learning_objective: State that spermatogenesis requires a sub-core testicular temperature of about 32 C.
